transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-03-12
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alice Nguyen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Stratos Head of ML), Ravi Kapoor (Stratos Platform), Noah Lopez (Stratos Product)

Summary: Demo focused on Redwood's Eval/Quality Monitoring features. Samir walked through prompt set upload, metric definitions, regression alert rules, and A/B comparison dashboards in the Console; Alice covered pricing and deployment tradeoffs. Customer asked about data residency, SOC 2, and how to surface false positive regression alerts.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alice Nguyen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining — we can probably do 40-ish minutes, we have a deck and then Samir will share a live console walkthrough. Maya, thanks for coordinating.
[00:08] Maya Chen: Yeah thanks Alice, excited to see how you guys flag regressions. We're starting to see some drift with our recommendation prompts.
[00:15] Samir Patel: Awesome, quick context from our side — Redwood's Eval product ties prompt sets to evaluation metrics; you can run continuous checks and receive regression alerts when metric deltas cross thresholds. We also support A/B comparisons across model versions and quantization profiles.
[00:32] Ravi Kapoor: Quick question — does this run in our VPC if we go private, or would data hit Redwood's hosted API?
[00:38] Alice Nguyen: Good question. You can run Eval in hosted mode where the console stores metadata and runs tests on our infra, or in Private where the evaluation runners live in your VPC and results stay in your environment. Both can push alerts to your SSO/SNS.
[00:55] Noah Lopez: And the alerting cadence — like we want hourly for critical templates and daily for lower pri — is that configurable?
[01:02] Samir Patel: Yep that's configurable. You can set per-prompt-set alert windows, severity levels, and integrate with PagerDuty/Slack.
[01:12] Maya Chen: Show us the prompt set flow — we have 200 prompts and a bunch of hinted labels, and we want to track accuracy + hallucination rate.
[01:21] Samir Patel: Sure I'll share screen — bear with me while I load the console — okay here we are, Eval tab, "Prompt Sets". You can upload CSV/JSONL, or point to S3. We automatically infer columns but you can map label fields.
[01:41] [01:42] Samir Patel (screen): uploading a sample — oh small typo in our UI but you get the idea — mapping 'expected_response' to the ground truth column.
[01:56] Samir Patel: For metrics we have token-level BLEU, exact-match, semantic similarity (embedding-based), and a hallucination detector that's model-agnostic. You can also add custom metrics computed from your scripts via a webhook.
[02:12] Maya Chen: That hallucination detector — how does it define hallucination? Is it model-specific?
[02:16] Samir Patel: It's mostly an alignment of semantic similarity to the reference plus heuristics tuned on our retail dataset; it's not perfect — expect false positives — but we expose thresholds and sample-level explanations so you can triage.
[02:36] Maya Chen: Ok, that'd help. Also, we need to compare across v1 (our current fine-tuned model) vs v2 (new quantized baseline) to see whether quantization is introducing regression.
[02:48] Samir Patel: That's exactly the A/B flow — you create an experiment, pick two model artifacts (or pinned variants), and the dashboard shows metric deltas, statistical significance, and per-prompt breakdowns.
[03:02] Ravi Kapoor: How do we get model outputs into Redwood's eval runners? We host models in our infra behind private endpoints.
[03:09] Samir Patel: You can either push outputs via the API — POST the outputs and expected — or we can run the requests against your private endpoints when using Private Eval. For hosted eval against our hosted models, we call internally and store both outputs and tokens.
[03:26] Noah Lopez: What's the overhead on running these checks — cost wise? If we run hourly on 200 prompts with 2 variants, that's a lot of tokens.
[03:35] Alice Nguyen: Good call — pricing differs by hosted vs private. Hosted eval is usage-based per evaluation token + storage for prompt sets and results; Dedicated/Private has a flat runner cost and you'd measure cost in runner hours. I'll send the hosted vs dedicated TCO spreadsheet after this call.
[03:52] Maya Chen: Can you do a quick demo of a regression alert email and the triage UX?
[03:57] Samir Patel: Yep — here's an alert list — you see "Hallucination increased" flagged for template "product_short_desc_v3" — click in and you get the sample list, side-by-side outputs, similarity score, and a suggested cause. You can mark false positives and those feed back into model-level suppression rules.
[04:24] [04:25] Samir Patel (typing): I'm going to run an A/B now with a small sample of 30 prompts to show differences — running... okay results are in — you can see mean exact-match changed from 0.84 to 0.78, p-value 0.03.
[04:45] Maya Chen: Hmm p-value 0.03 — that's concerning. Can I drill to outlier prompts?
[04:49] Samir Patel: Click the "Outliers" tab — here's per-prompt delta, with link to original tickets if you want to open triage tasks directly into Jira.
[05:05] Ravi Kapoor: How are we storing PII or sensitive prompts? Do you redact?
[05:11] Alice Nguyen: We support redaction pipelines before ingestion, and when using Private Eval, data never leaves your VPC. For hosted, we have retention controls and support customer-managed keys for storage encryption. We can share SOC 2 and encryption docs after the call.
[05:32] Maya Chen: Great — about false positives — we can't have ops chasing every alert. How do we control noise?
[05:37] Samir Patel: Two levers: adjust alert thresholds and require X correlated metrics to trigger (for example, similarity drop AND hallucination increase), and use sample suppression rules where labeled false positives reduce future alerts on similar patterns.
[05:52] Noah Lopez: For our pilot, we want to test hosted eval for speed, but if results look promising we'll move to Private for data governance. Timeline target is end of Q2.
[06:03] Alice Nguyen: Sounds reasonable. Pilot plan suggestion: 1) Stratos shares 200 prompts + rubric, 2) Redwood runs baseline eval on current v1 and v2, 3) we review results and tune alert thresholds, 4) if good, spin up Private runner for continuous checks.
[06:21] Maya Chen: That roadmap works. A few more quick technicals — can eval handle streaming outputs and partial tokens? Our recommender returns streamed completions for latency reasons.
[06:30] Samir Patel: We capture streamed tokens and can compute metrics on final outputs; we store the prefix KV metadata too when using our runtime. Slight caveat: some streaming metrics like per-token latency are best measured in Dedicated because of network variability.
[06:48] Ravi Kapoor: Do you have integrations for our observability stack? We use Datadog and S3 for artifacts.
[06:54] Samir Patel: Yep Datadog, Slack, PagerDuty, and results export to S3 or a webhook. You can also push raw eval artifacts to your S3 via connector.
[07:10] [07:11] Alice Nguyen: Quick note on A/B comparisons — we do sample size estimation for significance so you don't over-interpret small deltas. The console warns when n<30 per arm.
[07:24] Maya Chen: Good. One compliance question — do you retain logs of original prompts? We need to comply with our retention policy and audit logs.
[07:31] Alice Nguyen: Retention is configurable; for hosted you can pick retention windows and we keep audit logs which are exportable. Private keeps everything in your environment. We'll send the SOC2 pack and retention docs.
[07:47] Noah Lopez: Any known limitations with quantized models? We want to know if a small drop is just quant noise.
[07:55] Samir Patel: We recommend paired A/B with per-prompt breakdown; often quantization shows consistent small deltas across many prompts. If it's sporadic, it's probably a data/seed difference. Our optimizer (Optimize) can recommend quant profiles that balance cost vs accuracy.
[08:12] Maya Chen: Can Optimize suggest batching/quant profiles per workload automatically?
[08:16] Samir Patel: Yes, Optimize uses historical traffic and your prompt-set evals to recommend batching sizes, KV cache configs, and quantization profiles. We showed that in a different demo — happy to include that in the pilot scope.
[08:28] Ravi Kapoor: For the pilot, what's the minimal work for our infra team? They don't want to manage new services.
[08:34] Alice Nguyen: Minimal path: provide S3 access to prompts and point Redwood to your private endpoints (for Private runner) or just upload outputs via API (for hosted). We can do most of the onboarding. For Dedicated runners, we provision a dedicated pool and work with your infra to open a few inbound rules.
[08:52] Maya Chen: Ok good. Can you write up the pilot SOW?
[08:55] Alice Nguyen: We'll draft a short SOW and timeline and include a success criteria checklist — mostly: detection rate on known regressions, false positive rate under X%, dashboarding set up.
[09:06] Noah Lopez: Anything else on security? We need SAML SSO and RBAC, plus SCIM provisioning.
[09:12] Alice Nguyen: Supported — SAML SSO, SCIM, role-based access, and audit trails are all supported. We'll attach the admin guide.
[09:22] Maya Chen: Great. One more nit — can we do a live run end-to-end during the pilot? Like upload prompts and trigger an alert within a day?
[09:29] Samir Patel: Yes — in the pilot we typically run an initial baseline and then schedule a synthetic regression to validate the alerting pipeline; that can be done within 24-48 hours once we have prompts and endpoints.
[09:42] Alice Nguyen: Ok folks, quick recap of next steps — I'll send pricing/TCO and SOW, Samir will run baseline eval when Maya uploads prompt set, Maya will share prompts and rubric. Any blockers?
[09:55] Maya Chen: No blockers, timing depends on legal sign-off but we'll aim to share prompts by Friday.
[10:01] Alice Nguyen: Perfect thanks everyone — we'll follow up with notes and docs.

End of transcript (approx 42 minutes).
questions: Can Eval run inside our VPC/private runner?
How are hallucinations defined and can false positives be suppressed?
What's the hosted vs dedicated TCO for hourly prompt checks?
Can we compare quantized vs non-quantized models with per-prompt deltas?
